opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most common objections I hear, and I understand where it comes from. The worry is something like: "If you get the careful company to be more careful, all you've done is slow them down relative to the careless one, so what's the point?" I think that framing is too pessimistic, for a few reasons.

First, I don't think safety practices are mostly about slowing down. A lot of what I'd want companies to do is relatively cheap: better information security, so your model weights don't get stolen; better evaluations, so you actually know what your systems can do; better alignment and control techniques, so if you do have a dangerous system, you've got some chance of catching problems. Many of these aren't huge competitive taxes. They're more like doing your homework. So the trade-off between "be safe" and "stay competitive" is often less stark than people assume.

Second, there's a demonstration effect. If one company develops a practice and shows it's workable, that lowers the cost for everyone else. It becomes something you can point to: "Look, this company does it and they're still at the frontier." That's how a lot of norms get established. You start with the most willing actors, the practice gets refined and cheaper, and it becomes something regulators, investors, employees, and the public can expect. The less safety-conscious companies may never adopt it voluntarily, but it becomes much easier to require.

Third, the companies are not all equally important at every moment. If the most capable systems are being built by a handful of companies, and some of those are reasonably safety-conscious, then improving their practices matters a lot even if a laggard doesn't follow. The question isn't "Is every actor safe?" It's "What's the risk from the systems that actually matter most, at the time they matter?"

And fourth, I think about it in terms of reducing risk at the margin rather than achieving guaranteed safety. A world where the leading developers have strong security, serious evaluations, and real plans for what to do if they see warning signs is meaningfully safer than one where nobody does, even if there's a reckless actor out there. You've reduced the number of dangerous points of failure, and you've built up the knowledge and infrastructure you'd need if governments eventually want to act.

So I'd say the uneven commitment across companies is a real limitation. It's a reason not to rely on voluntary corporate practices as the whole plan. But it's not a reason to think they're worthless. I think of them as one important layer: they buy down risk directly, and they lay the groundwork for broader standards and regulation that can reach the actors who wouldn't move on their own.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uneven safety commitments and company practices but does not use animal welfare as an analogy.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says a world where leading developers have strong safety measures is meaningfully safer than one where nobody does, even with reckless actors.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and I think the honest answer is that it's complicated, and I don't want to pretend it's not.

The first thing I'd say is that even in a world where there's a lot of heterogeneity in how much companies care about safety, improving practices at the companies that do care is still valuable, because those companies are plausibly going to be among the ones that end up with the most powerful systems. It's not like the safety-focused companies are irrelevant to the outcome. If one of them is at or near the frontier, then what they do matters a lot, and raising the bar there is a direct contribution.

But I think the more interesting part of the question is about the spillover effects. And here I'd break it into a few pieces.

One is that practices tend to diffuse. If one company develops a reasonably rigorous way of doing dangerous capability evaluations, or a way of thinking about when to pause, or a security standard, that becomes a thing other companies can copy, and it becomes a thing that customers, employees, journalists, and governments can point to and say, "Why aren't you doing this?" A lot of what ends up as industry norm or eventually regulation starts as something one company did voluntarily. So you're not just improving one company; you're changing what "normal" looks like.

A second piece is that I think the picture of "some companies care and some don't" is a bit too static. Companies are made of people, and the people change, and the leadership changes, and the commercial and political pressures change. A company that looks cavalier today could be in a very different position in a couple of years if there's been a serious incident or if the regulatory environment has shifted. If there's a well-developed playbook sitting there, they can adopt it much faster than if they'd have to invent it from scratch. So part of the value of the work is in creating options for a future where more actors want to do the right thing.

A third piece, and this is where I'd be more cautious, is that I do think there's a real risk of a kind of complacency or "safety-washing" dynamic, where the fact that some companies have nice-sounding frameworks makes it seem like the problem is handled, and that reduces pressure for the kind of external, enforceable requirements that would actually bind everyone. I take that seriously. My view is that the response to that isn't to stop improving the practices at the responsible companies; it's to be clear-eyed that voluntary commitments are not the end state, and to put real effort into the things that would apply to everyone, like government capacity, standards, international coordination, that sort of thing.

And then the last thing I'd say is that I think there's often an implicit framing where the question is, "Is this intervention sufficient to make the world safe?" And by that standard almost nothing passes. The standard I'd use is more like, "Does this move things in the right direction at reasonable cost, and does it foreclose other things we'd want to do?" Improving safety practices at the companies that are receptive seems to me like it clearly passes that bar. It doesn't solve the problem of the companies that aren't receptive, and I wouldn't want anyone to think it does. But I'd rather have a world where the best practices are really good and some actors aren't following them than a world where nobody has figured out what good practices even look like.

r001.rationale: The response discusses differences in companies’ safety practices but does not use animal welfare as an analogy.

r002.rationale: It says improving receptive companies’ practices is valuable and preferable to having no established best practices, but does not state that this would make the world substantially safer.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a temptation to say, “Well, if one company is going to be reckless, what does it matter whether the others are careful?” And I don’t think that’s the right way to think about it.

For one thing, it matters who’s ahead. If a company with better safety practices is setting the pace, that could put us in a much better position than if a company with worse practices is setting the pace. So improving the practices of a particular company can be valuable even if you can’t improve everyone’s practices at once.

But also, companies don’t make these decisions in isolation. If one company develops good ways of evaluating dangerous capabilities, or makes a credible commitment to what it will do when it sees them, that makes it easier to ask other companies to do the same. It gives policymakers something concrete to work with. It can help turn “we should be safe” into an actual standard that people can understand and apply.

That doesn’t mean voluntary commitments solve the whole problem. If the risk is large enough, you ultimately want some way of constraining actors who aren’t willing to be careful. But I see improving individual companies’ practices as potentially helping us get there, as well as having direct value. I wouldn’t write it off just because some companies care less.

r001.rationale: The response does not use animal welfare as an analogy.

r002.rationale: It says better practices at the leading company could put us in a better position than worse practices setting the pace, but it does not compare that world with one where nobody makes efforts to improve AI safety practices.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to ask what the improvement actually buys you. If one company becomes more cautious, but another company is going to do the same dangerous thing six months later, that limits the benefit. You can’t just look at the first company in isolation and say, “We made it safer, so we’ve solved that piece of the problem.”

But I also wouldn’t conclude that improving safety practices at individual companies is pointless. A company can develop evaluations or techniques that other companies adopt. It can demonstrate that a particular precaution is workable. And it can help establish a standard that eventually becomes an industry expectation or a regulatory requirement.

So I’d distinguish between making one company more willing to slow down and making the whole situation safer. Those can overlap, but they aren’t identical. I’m especially interested in practices that can spread, and in arrangements where companies have some confidence that their competitors will take similar precautions. The question is less “How safety-conscious is this company?” and more “How does changing its behavior affect the risks across the whole field?”

r001.rationale: The response does not use animal welfare as an analogy.

r002.rationale: It says company-level improvements can spread and are not pointless, but does not clearly state that a world with stronger measures at leading companies would be substantially safer than a world with no effort to improve safety practices.
